questions.q: What does a container virtualize, according to this lesson?
options: A full guest operating system with its own kernel, on top of a hypervisor
An isolated process that shares the host machine's kernel
Nothing — a container is just a compressed folder of files
A separate physical server
questions.explain: A container is an isolated process with its own filesystem and network interface, but it shares the host's kernel rather than booting its own.

questions.q: Why does a virtual machine typically take a minute or more to start, versus about a second for a comparable container?
options: Virtual machines are always run on remote, higher-latency servers
Virtual machines use slower storage hardware
A VM boots an entire guest operating system and kernel on a hypervisor, which a container skips
Containers are always smaller files than virtual machine disk images
questions.explain: The VM has to boot a full guest OS and kernel; a container just starts an isolated process on the kernel that's already running.

questions.q: What specific problem do containers solve for AI projects, per this lesson?
options: They package an exact Python version, CUDA/PyTorch build, and dependency stack as one artifact that runs identically everywhere
They automatically improve model accuracy during training
They eliminate the need for a GPU entirely
They make a model's weight files smaller
questions.explain: The 'it worked on my machine' problem — mismatched Python, CUDA, and package versions — is exactly what a container's packaged runtime and dependencies solve.

questions.q: What does the Docker Desktop Containers view screenshot in this lesson actually show?
options: Source code for the Docker Engine
A list of virtual machines, each running its own kernel
A conceptual diagram with no relationship to a real deployment
Several real, isolated containers running side by side, each with its own image, ports, and CPU usage
questions.explain: It's a genuine Docker Desktop screenshot, not an illustration — each row is a real running (or stopped) container.

questions.q: In the build log screenshot, what does each executing instruction actually become in the final image?
options: A separate running container
Its own layer on disk, added in order
A network request to Docker Hub
A new virtual machine
questions.explain: The build log shows instructions executing one at a time, and each one becomes its own layer in the resulting image — the subject of Lesson 3.
